diagnostics.title: Buffer pool: full or warming
diagnostics.headline: Warming: 7% full, about 12 min 17 s to full at this rate
diagnostics.verdict: The buffer pool is still filling: 6.7% of it is in use (7,566 of 8,112 pages are free). Data pages grew by 82 in the window (8.18 pages per second, 130.8 KiB/s). At this rate it is full in about 12 min 17 s. That is an estimate: the fill rate follows the workload. Reads from disk are expected while it warms.
diagnostics.why: InnoDB keeps a small free list: once free pages drop below half of innodb_lru_scan_depth, the page cleaner evicts the least recently used pages until there are innodb_lru_scan_depth free pages again (MariaDB has one buffer pool instance) (1,536 x 1 = 1,536 pages here). So "full" means free pages at or below that target, not zero. Once it is full, every page read from disk evicts another one. Bytes read from disk are the pages read from disk times innodb_page_size (16.0 KiB); MariaDB's Innodb_buffer_pool_reads already includes read-ahead, so nothing is added. Innodb_data_read counts the bytes InnoDB read from its data files: it is lower for ROW_FORMAT=COMPRESSED tables, which read the smaller compressed page.
diagnostics.rule: full when free pages are at or below innodb_lru_scan_depth x buffer pool instances (the free list InnoDB's page cleaner keeps). Full: ok below 10 pages read from disk per second, watch at 10 or more, problem when the hit ratio is also below 95%. Not full: no threshold

diagnostics.title: Redo log size for the write rate
diagnostics.headline: Covers about 46 min 11 s of writes
diagnostics.verdict: At this window's rate (35.5 KiB/s, about 124.7 MiB per hour) the 96.0 MiB redo capacity holds about 46 min 11 s of writes. That is less than the hour a common rule of thumb aims for at peak. The checkpoint age is 561.2 KiB (1% of the capacity); at this rate InnoDB starts flushing ahead in about 32 min 10 s.
diagnostics.why: InnoDB writes every change to the redo log first. A checkpoint frees redo space once the matching dirty pages are flushed, so the capacity limits how far flushing can fall behind. The checkpoint age (Innodb_checkpoint_age) is how much of the redo log is in use. MariaDB starts flushing ahead at 7/8 of Innodb_checkpoint_max_age (about 71% of innodb_log_file_size) and makes writes wait at Innodb_checkpoint_max_age (about 81%). A larger redo log smooths that out but makes crash recovery longer. MariaDB's Innodb_os_log_written is the growth of the log sequence number since startup (the redo generated), not the bytes written to the file, so one counter serves both. Innodb_log_waits counts waits for space in the in-memory log buffer (innodb_log_buffer_size), a different limit.
diagnostics.rule: watch when the checkpoint age reaches 7/8 of Innodb_checkpoint_max_age (flushing ahead) in either sample, problem at Innodb_checkpoint_max_age (writes wait); also watch when the capacity holds less than about 1 hour of redo at this window's rate (a common rule of thumb; this window may not be the peak) or when Innodb_log_waits grew

numbers.label: Capacity covers
numbers.text: about 46 min 11 s of writes at this rate

numbers.label: Time until InnoDB flushes ahead, at this rate
numbers.text: about 32 min 10 s (from the current checkpoint age to 67.4 MiB)

recommendation.text: If this rate is typical of busy periods, about an hour of redo at it is 256.0 MiB (rounded up to 256 MiB): SET GLOBAL innodb_log_file_size = 268435456; resizes it online (the statement waits until the resize finishes); also set it in the configuration file so a restart keeps it.
recommendation.caveat: One short window may be a burst or a lull: compare several refreshes, or the Config tab's average since startup. A larger redo log uses more disk and makes crash recovery longer.

diagnostics.title: Table open cache
diagnostics.headline: No misses
diagnostics.verdict: No overflows in the window: the tables in use fit in the cache. 0.0% of 2,810 lookups missed. 17 of 2,000 cached instances are open.
diagnostics.why: Each statement needs an open instance of every table it uses. A hit reuses a free instance from the cache. A miss opens a new one (Opened_tables): the first use of a table, or another session needing its own instance of a busy table, so misses alone are normal. An overflow means the cache was full and an unused instance was closed to make room (if one existed; otherwise the instance grows): tables are being opened and closed over and over. On MariaDB each active instance (Table_open_cache_active_instances, up to table_open_cache_instances) holds up to table_open_cache tables, so Open_tables can exceed table_open_cache.
diagnostics.rule: watch at 1 overflow per second, problem at 10, with at least 5 in the window. Misses without overflows are not judged

diagnostics.title: Table definition cache
diagnostics.headline: 0 opened per second
diagnostics.verdict: 0 table definitions were opened in the window (0 per second); 23 of 400 are cached.
diagnostics.why: The definition cache keeps parsed table definitions (shares), separate from the open table instances. A definition is opened the first time a table is used, or again after it was evicted because the cache was full. Steady openings while the cache is full mean table_definition_cache is smaller than the number of tables in use.
diagnostics.rule: watch when table definitions are opened at 1 per second or more (at least 5 in the window) while the definition cache is at least 95% full

diagnostics.title: Thread cache
diagnostics.headline: 3 new connections
diagnostics.verdict: Only 3 new connections in the window, too few to judge the thread cache.
diagnostics.why: With one thread per connection, the server keeps up to thread_cache_size idle threads to reuse for new connections; Threads_created counts the threads it had to create instead. Connections is the next thread id: every connection that got past the max_connections check (failed logins included), plus a few internal threads. Each window includes this tool's own connection.
diagnostics.rule: watch when more than 10% of new connections needed a new thread, with threads created at 1 per second or more (at least 5 in the window); never a problem

numbers.label: Connections that reused a cached thread
Idle threads in the cache now

diagnostics.title: Binary log cache
diagnostics.headline: Binary log off
diagnostics.verdict: The binary log is off (log_bin=OFF), so there is no binary log cache to check.
diagnostics.why: With the binary log on, each session collects a transaction's events in memory (binlog_cache_size; binlog_stmt_cache_size for changes to non-transactional tables) and writes them to the binary log at commit. Events that do not fit spill to a temporary file on disk (Binlog_cache_disk_use, Binlog_stmt_cache_disk_use); on MariaDB 12.3 and later with binlog_storage_engine set, they spill into the binary log itself and still count. The cache is per session, so a larger size is multiplied by the sessions that write.
diagnostics.rule: No threshold: compare with this server's usual values

diagnostics.title: Open files
diagnostics.headline: 0.1% of open_files_limit
diagnostics.verdict: At least 42 file descriptors are in use: 30 through the server's file layer, 11 InnoDB files and 1 connection, 0.1% of open_files_limit 32,198.
diagnostics.why: open_files_limit is the most file descriptors the server process can hold. Open_files counts files the server opened through its own file layer (MyISAM and Aria tables, binary and relay logs, some temporary files), not InnoDB's, which Innodb_num_open_files counts; each client connection also uses a socket. myflames adds the three, a lower bound: other descriptors are not visible through SQL.
diagnostics.rule: watch when the file descriptors myflames can account for reach 75% of open_files_limit, problem at 90%

diagnostics.title: Rows read by full scans
diagnostics.headline: 53,505 rows/s by sequential scans
diagnostics.verdict: Storage engines returned 53,505 rows per second to sequential scans, 72.0% of all rows read through handlers.
diagnostics.why: Handler_read_rnd_next counts requests for the next row of a sequential table scan, so a high rate points at full table scans. It also counts scans of internal temporary tables (GROUP BY, DISTINCT, derived tables, UNION), and this tool's own SHOW GLOBAL STATUS reads about 600 rows that way per window (measured), so it is an upper bound on rows from full scans of user tables. Full index scans count in Handler_read_first and Handler_read_next instead. Top statements shows which statements scan.
diagnostics.rule: No threshold: compare with this server's usual values

numbers.label: Share of all rows read through handlers

diagnostics.title: Temporary tables on disk
diagnostics.headline: 99.9% of 703 on disk
diagnostics.verdict: 702 of 703 internal temporary tables in the window were on disk (99.9%).
diagnostics.why: Internal temporary tables (GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION, derived tables) start in memory and move to disk when they outgrow the limit. MariaDB keeps each internal temporary table in memory up to the smaller of tmp_memory_table_size (tmp_table_size is its alias) and max_heap_table_size (16.0 MiB); larger ones, and ones with BLOB or TEXT columns, go to Aria tables on disk. MariaDB counts a table that starts in memory and moves to disk twice in Created_tmp_tables, so the share understates moves to disk.
diagnostics.rule: watch at 10% on disk, problem at 25%; with fewer than 20 temporary tables in the window, watch at most

numbers.label: Created on disk or moved there

recommendation.text: Find the statements with the temporary-table-on-disk flag in Top statements; an index that avoids the temporary table helps more than a bigger limit. Then raise the limit for the sessions that need it (SET SESSION tmp_table_size = <bytes>; max_heap_table_size too).
recommendation.caveat: Each concurrent temporary table can use up to the limit, so a large global value risks memory pressure. Tables with BLOB or TEXT columns go to disk regardless.

diagnostics.title: Sorts that spill to disk
diagnostics.headline: 1,421 merge passes for 702 sorts
diagnostics.verdict: 1,421 merge passes in the window for 702 sorts.
diagnostics.why: A sort that cannot use an index (filesort) collects rows in sort_buffer_size. When they do not fit, it writes sorted runs to a temporary file and merges them, and each merge pass is counted in Sort_merge_passes. Sort_range and Sort_scan count the sorts themselves. sort_buffer_size is a limit for each sort in every session, so raise it for the sessions that need it rather than globally.
diagnostics.rule: watch at 1 per second, problem at 10 per second, with at least 5 in the window

recommendation.text: Find the sorting statements in Top statements first: an index in ORDER BY or GROUP BY order removes the sort. For the rest, raise sort_buffer_size per session (SET SESSION sort_buffer_size = <bytes>).
recommendation.caveat: A large global sort_buffer_size lets every concurrent sort use up to that much memory.

metrics.label: Dirty pages
metrics.explain: Pages changed in memory and not yet flushed to disk, as a share of the buffer pool. Near innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct (90%) InnoDB flushes harder. A high share alone is not a stall; waits for a free page and a nearly full redo log are. MariaDB's page cleaner can stay idle below the maximum by default (innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct_lwm 0), so a healthy server can sit near it.
metrics.why: 404 of 8,112 pages are dirty. Rule of thumb: watch at innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct; a high share alone is not a stall, waits for a free page and a nearly full redo log are.
metrics.rule: watch at innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct; a high share alone is not a stall, waits for a free page and a nearly full redo log are

metrics.label: Free pages
metrics.explain: Empty pages ready for new reads. A busy server's buffer pool is usually full, which is normal: InnoDB evicts the least recently used pages. Waits for a free page are the signal.
metrics.why: 7,566 of 8,112 pages are free. No threshold: compare with this server's usual values.

metrics.label: Waits for a free page
metrics.explain: Times a session found no free page, even after scanning the LRU list, so it had to flush a page or wait (Innodb_buffer_pool_wait_free; MariaDB counts each one-second wait for the page cleaner). The page cleaner is not keeping up, or the buffer pool is small for the workload.
metrics.why: 0 waits in 10 s (0 per second). Rule of thumb: watch when any occur in the window, problem at 1 per second or more.
metrics.rule: watch when any occur in the window, problem at 1 per second or more

metrics.label: Time waiting for row locks
metrics.explain: Milliseconds of row lock waiting per second of wall time (Innodb_row_lock_time, added when each wait ends). 1,000 ms per second means one session waited the whole time. A long wait that ends in the window adds all of its time here.
metrics.why: 5,481 ms of waiting ended in the window. Rule of thumb: watch at 100 ms of waiting per second, problem at 1,000 ms per second (one session always waiting).
metrics.rule: watch at 100 ms of waiting per second, problem at 1,000 ms per second (one session always waiting)

metrics.label: Average row lock wait
metrics.explain: Wait time that ended in the window divided by the waits that started in it. Waits that span the window's edges make it approximate. MariaDB rounds each wait down to whole milliseconds.
metrics.why: 5,481 ms over 1 waits. Rule of thumb: watch at 50 ms per wait, problem at 1 s per wait.
metrics.rule: watch at 50 ms per wait, problem at 1 s per wait

metrics.label: Redo generated
metrics.explain: Redo log generated per second (Innodb_os_log_written, the redo generated since startup on MariaDB). MySQL's adaptive flushing reaches its age limit when the checkpoint age is about 73% of the redo capacity, and MariaDB flushes ahead from 7/8 of Innodb_checkpoint_max_age (about 71% of innodb_log_file_size), so the time shown runs from the current checkpoint age to that point. Writes stall if the log fills before a checkpoint frees it.
metrics.why: 355.7 KiB of redo in the window. No threshold: compare with this server's usual values.
metrics.detail: flush-ahead starts in about 32 min 10 s at this rate (checkpoint age 561.2 KiB of 96.0 MiB)

notes: The server started 14 s ago. Its buffer pool may still be warming up, so disk reads are expected to be higher than usual.

Statuses are rules of thumb, not verdicts; each metric and diagnostic says which rule it uses. Each window includes this tool's own second sample: about 3 statements, with the temporary table and scans they need, and its connection.
